newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa oil industry urges clarity on govt policy.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa oil industry urges clarity on govt policy.

text.p: The uncertainty about the government's planned new liquid fuels policy must end this year if investment to meet future demand is to materialise on time, the South African oil industry warned on Monday.
In its latest annual report the South African Petroleum Industry Association (Sapia) warned repeatedly that after three years of uncertainty, the sector was in limbo.
"This year the impasse must end, and the industry be allowed to plan with certainty its future development," chairman Dennis Poole of Total South Africa (Pty) Ltd said.

Immediate past chairman Mike Rademeyer of Caltex Oil (SA) Pty Ltd said that in 1996 the industry had been left "idle in no-man's land", particularly by the government's failure to act on Sapia's application for a long overdue margin increase.
He said that although the net after tax income of Sapia members had risen to 1.4 billion rand in 1996 from 0.8 billion in 1995, the real outcome was in fact lower.

"If after-tax stock profits, arising from the increases in oil prices during 1996 of 0.6 billion rand are excluded from the 1996 income, net income after tax was 0.8 billion rand lower than the 0.9 billion rand of 1995," Rademeyer said.

"The combined marketing and refining after-tax return on assets of 7.9 percent, a figure which includes the stock profits, is insufficient to ensure that the necessary investments in the industry will be made. It is less than can be earned on a bank deposit."
Sapia director Colin McClelland said that although there was still adequate refining capacity for several years, the need for a clear policy was becoming urgent.
It was estimated that refining capacity for gasoline would slide into a shortfall of 575 million litres by the year 2000, given low economic growth, and 1,591 million litres, given high growth.
Refining capacity for diesel would remain in surplus beyond that date.
Rademeyer said some might suggest that new investors would invest in the needed expanded capacity if Sapia members did not.
"We, however, doubt that new investors will be attracted by the returns currently available in this industry," he said.
This did not mean that the industry had not been investing and Rademeyer said that 1.4 billion rand had been invested in 1996, but mainly in marketing assets.
"It is future multi-billion rand refining investments which are at stake due to the current uncertainty," Poole said.
In a foreword to the report, Minerals and Energy Minister Penuell Maduna said work was continuing on a new policy paper for the industry, but he gave no indication of when it would be completed.

Several commissions and studies on possible policy options have been commissioned over the last few years. The situation has been exacerbated by the fact that the previous minister, the National Party's Pik Botha, was replaced by Maduna last year when the NP left the government of national unity. Maduna then started his own policy process from scratch.
Sapia members are BP Southern Africa (Pty) Ltd, Caltex Oil (SA) (Pty) Ltd, Engen Petroleum Ltd, Shell SA (Pty) Ltd, Total South Africa (Pty) Ltd and Zenex Oil (Pty) Ltd.
